blocks.x: This is Bill Russell interviewing Mr. David Oxley at 732 St. Peter Street, and the date is January the 6th, 1965. Do you want to give your full name?
My name is David Samuel Oxley, Sr.
You have a boy of the same name.
That's right, boy, Jr. David Samuel Oxley, Jr.
Do you mind telling just when you were born, your birth date and the year and the date and all?
Well, I was born on the 1st of May, 1910, on a Sunday morning at 730, my mother told me.
Where was it? Over right here in this side of the river?
That's right, up in Carlton.
Up in Carlton, way up by it.
Out in between Oak and Zimple.
Yeah, was that almost a separate town in those days, I guess? Oh, yeah. Can you tell us about your family a little, if they played music, your father and mother?

Well, I had an uncle that told me, used to try to play trumpet. But I mean, he didn't care too much, you know what I mean, about it. In other words, he wasn't a professional musician. Yeah. And so I don't know of anybody else in my family that played music.
You didn't play in any of the bands then, that anybody around remembers him much in any band?
No. No. No.
And your father didn't play anything then?
No, he didn't play any instruments at all.
Your mother sang or anything? I guess they all sang a little bit.
Oh, yeah. They were great singers. They used to have quartets and different things like that, you know.
Yeah.
They were great singers, I mean. But so far as playing music, well, I don't remember any one of them playing music.
Can you remember the first music you ever heard where it was or what kind of, was it bands or parades or music in churches or home or place?
Well, I used to hear a lot of bands. I mean, these parades, you know what I mean, and different things like that, and the second lines. I used to follow the parade when I was a little kid.
How long did you live in Carlton?

Did you live there for years? Well, yeah, for years. I lived in Carlton until I was old enough to, you know, go out on my own, most likely. Of course, we lived around, you know, different sections of the city, too, you know.
Yeah.
We moved in different places, you know. And then we ended up right back up in Carlton again.
What was the first instrument you played? Did you start on drums or...?
Well, I tell you, I started my career as a drummer beating on the steps. You see, like these box steps they have?
Yeah, a lot of kids. Kicking the side of the box.
Yeah. Used to take the rounds off a chair, you know what I mean? Yeah.
Made drumsticks out of that.
And whistle a tune, you know, and kick the side of the step.
That was your bass drum. Bass drumming. Played this. Yeah, pretty good. That's right. How old were you, I guess, just a little kid when you started doing that?
Well, I imagine I must have been around about six or seven years old, somewhere along.
When did you get your first drum set? Can you remember that?
Well, I remember I bought my first drum set when I was around about 14 years old.
Did you get the whole set or just the snare or something first?
First I bought the snare, then I bought the stand and the bass drum, you know what I mean? So it touched like that.
Had you wanted to play in a band then or were you with some other kids that needed a drummer? How come you started on drums?

Well, I'll tell you. We had one of those old graphophones, you know, the graphophones with a big horn, you know. My daddy used to buy the records of Celestine and King Oliver and those fellas, you know.
I remember those old records, yeah.
And I used to set up my drums in the front room and play along with the records, you see, when they played, see. Oh, yeah. Celestine and those bands.
Yeah.
And I finally used to play with Celestine, you know. Yeah. Yeah.
Can you remember any of the other records you played with, what they were?
Well, I'll tell you.
Titles or anything? I know it's hard to remember back that far.

Well, I remember one, let's see, the Wolverine Blues was one, I know. And there was another one they used to call, oh, let's see, what this, what like the Tin Roof Blues, you know. Numbers like that, I mean, like Louis Armstrong.
Oh, yeah, there were a lot of those, so hundreds of those numbers like that, I guess.
You see, my mother used to have, they used to have what have known as fish fries on a Saturday night, you know.
Oh, yeah, I've heard of that.
They'd send us to get fish, and, you know, they'd fry fish on Saturday, and they used to sell home breweries.
That would be up in your home then.
It would be in my home, see, and I'd put on these records, you know, and I'd play music.
Play with them.
Everybody around the neighborhood, you know, would be out there listening at the band, and come in and buy us a fish, you know, buy us a home brewery.

Yeah, Sing Miller was up here a couple weeks ago telling about the fish fries too, and he used to play for them. And he imagined sometime, if they didn't have a piano player, they'd just use a phonograph too.
That's right, use the phonograph and the drummer. That's right.
Yeah, pretty good. Did you play in any school bands then, or did they have any music in your school, if you remember?
No, no, we never had a piano, you know, their voices singing, you know.
What school did you go to?
Well, I went to McDonough No. 24.
Is it up there? Tom Lafon. Up in Carlton.
Well, yeah, McDonough 24 was in Carlton, and I mean, we had to walk around about 18 blocks of school, man. I mean, there wasn't no such a thing as school buses, you know.

I wonder if that's the school Mahalia Jackson went to. Same school. One of them up there. Same school. It's down near the river. Her church is on Milladon. That's right. And their school is only maybe near, yeah, right up in there. That's where. That's right. I've seen the school in a big white building. McDonough 24.
That's right. Same school.

Yeah. Can you tell us about your first jobs then when you did, or did you get a job very soon after you got your drums aside from the fish fry? I know that's your job too, in a way. Did you play with any band pretty soon?

Kids or anyone else? Well, when I was around about, oh, I was going into, I hadn't quite made my 15. I'm going into 15 years old. I was working down at Janky Dry Dock. And I was able to buy some more, you know what I mean? Other traps and accessories. Some traps to go with the drums, you see? And my first job was out at Millenburg.
Oh, yeah, out there at the lake. That's right.
Out there with Prince Miller, Bubba Green, and...
Let's see, Bubba Green, what did he play? I can't remember.
He was a clarinet player.
He played clarinet.
He played clarinet.
Some of the men, I don't remember. I never met him, so I just can't... The names aren't always familiar.

That's right. Well, he was from Ruppen-Carlton, too. He's a little old fellow now. Is he still living? Yeah, he's still living, they tell me. I haven't seen him in a long time. Does he play anymore? No, he doesn't play, I don't think.
Yeah, I guess that's why I never...
I haven't seen him in quite a while. And, well, Chris Kelly, it was Chris Kelly's band then. And we used to play out there on a Sunday. We used to ride this train going out there.
You used to call it Smokey Mary. I never got the state that everybody talks about. That's right.
We used to ride out there. They had different camps out there, you know.
Yeah, I've heard about them. They still had a few little things like that out there, like Mama Lou's and those kind that I saw. Yeah, that's right.

It used to be wonderful. I mean, people used to enjoy themselves so much out there. And the band would start playing maybe around about, say, 12 o'clock in the day. And you'd probably end up maybe around about 1 or 2 o'clock that Monday morning, you see.
Yeah.
So my daddy used to raise sand because I'd be out there too late. Yeah. He wanted me in at 9 o'clock at night.
It'd take a long time to get back up home then. That's right.
But I told him, I mean, playing music like that, where you couldn't be in at 9, see. So it was one of those things.
Any other early bands you can remember playing with or also the ones that you heard when you were about that age? Well... Who was your favorite drummer, for instance? Who did you ever watch or see?
My favorite drummer was a drummer at the Lyric Theater, which was Happy.
Yeah. Red Happy. That's right. Red Happy.
That was my favorite drummer.
Yeah. A lot of people talk about him.
That's right.
They forgot to see.

He was my favorite drummer. Well, after a while, I played around with a couple of bands, like, well, like Kid Howard. I played with Kid. And I was still a youngster. And I had an opportunity to leave home, to go on the road with a show. For my first job, I left here with Johnny Le Long and his playmates. On the Lyric Theater.
Le Long?
Johnny Le Long.
Yeah.
And his playmates.
What kind of a show was it? Oh, well, you know what I mean. Was he the star of it? I mean, I don't remember.
Well, he was the manager and he was on the show.
On the show. He was an actor or a singer or something or what?

Well, he used to do a straight. He was a straight man. He used to do a straight. And we was on this TOBA time, the Theatronors Booking Association. We played at towns like Mobile, Birmingham, Atlanta.
You know, he played the circuits, you see. You know, on up to New York and then back around again.

And most of the time he got to New York, well, that was the end of the line. He had to stay around there, maybe around about five or six months, maybe before you got another driver covered out, you know.
Did you hit Chicago, too, on that circuit? Yeah, Chicago. I know they didn't have theaters up there.

Yeah, we played the monogram. We used to play the monogram at 35th and State then. See, well, now they got the Regal. I mean, they had the Regal. There were different theaters. We used to play the monogram then.
I don't remember the monogram. I remember the Grand Theater there on State. That's right. It was about 31st. That's right. The monogram was about 35th.
35th and State. That's right.
Right. And the Vendome was in there, too. That's right. I remember that. They just tore that down in my time.
That's right. In Cincinnati, well, they had the Roosevelt there. In Cincinnati, you'd get off at the station and walk, well, about a block to the theater, you know.

Is it right in that section? Yeah. That's all torn down, too. Yeah, I never saw it before. I found it out when we went back in there. What other shows, then, did you work with? How long? Well, what year was that? When I was with John A. Lee Long?
That was in 1926.
26, back in the year.
You were pretty young then. Yeah, I was going on 16. 16 or something.
See, I made my 16 on the 1st of May. So I left town. It was during around about, oh, February or March.
Yeah.
I made my 16 on the road.
Anybody else in the band from New Orleans much that you can remember?
Well, not on that show. They needed a drummer, you see.
I was the only one that was on that show.
At that time, I was making $18. They started me off at $18 a week.
Yeah.
Then I had an act of my own, you know, jumping over the drums and different things.
Up on the stage, too. Yeah, on the stage.

And I kind of had taken some little things that Happy used to do, you know, on the bugle blues, you know. What did they do? I never got to see. He used to throw his sticks on the floor. Let them bounce. And bounce up. And on the brakes, he'd pull a string and a pistol would shoot. You know what I mean?
And a wing and all that kind of stuff, you know.
Well, I used to do all that little thing, too.
Yeah.
Using six sticks at the time, you know, and playing the cymbal behind my back. And walking around the drums, you know, playing and all that kind of stuff.
Those things go over big, usually. That's right. They do them right.
So they raised my cyrus to $25 a week. That was big money.
Yeah, for a kid that was only 16 or so.

Well, after I left Johnny Lee, I went with a carnival show, Miller's Midway shows. I stayed with Miller about, well, off and on. They'd go in winter quarters, you know, and come back out, you know what I mean, during the spring. Well, I stayed with Miller, I imagine around about two years. And we traveled, played different towns a week, staying in the towns a week, you know.
Yeah, did you hit very far away or just the towns around in the south, or where did you go?
Well, we played towns in the south. And with this show, particular show, went up for us, Kentucky, Tennessee, Missouri, like around up there, you know.
Was that a New Orleans band or just some of the fellas?
Well, they had some fellas from New Orleans on the show.
Anybody else from here, if you remember?
Well, there was a piano player from here, his name was Calvin Distance. He's dead. He was killed in St. Louis. I don't think he made any name here.
Records or any great name.
And a trombone player, they called him Jazz Baby.
He was from here?

Jazz was from here. Well, I mean, he stayed here a while, but he wasn't originally from here, you know. He came here and lived a while and he left with the show. Then Willie Humphrey's daddy was the band leader.
Oh, he was.
Willie, the old man. The old man. Played clarinet. Well, he was the band leader on that show. On this carnival. On this carnival. That's right.
I didn't know. We talked to him once after he had a stroke and he couldn't tell us very much. His memory wasn't really good then. Yeah, he was the band leader. He was very old.
That's right.
Just died last year, I believe, wasn't it? I think so, yeah.
That's right, last year. About a year ago.
He plays clarinet or did he play sax or what did he do?
He played clarinet. Clarinet. Strictly clarinet. That's what he played then.

And he was leader of the band. I didn't know that. Maybe he told us and I forgot. Then any other shows that came after that? Did you ever play here much in between? Did you ever play here in between the shows?
I first stayed away from here, I'd say, about seven years.
Yeah.

You see? Wiling around Pittsburgh, Baltimore, New York, Philadelphia around there, you know. Then I came back home here. When I came back, the first one I played with when I came back here, I think, was Kid Howard. I started playing with him. Then I played with Henry Russ. I played with Henry Horton's band. Then I left and I went on the road again. Yeah.
See?
And I came back again. I played with Jimmy Davis. And then I had a few of my own outfits, you know, a few of my own bands.
Any special jobs? Any, that is, it lasted a while, any certain places or clubs or just jobbing around for single engagements? How did you do it?
Well, I stayed at, played at the, at the, uh... stuff
When I was with Dave Tholomew, I played at the Robin Hood, and we played up at the, what's the name of this club up on Eagle Street. We stayed up there quite a while. At the Gravestone.
Yeah, I don't know what it was. I played at the Rhythm Club with Joe Roversho's band.
We stayed there quite a while. We used to broadcast from there nationwide and we'd broadcast from there. I've heard of that, that's right.
He told us about that too.
I played out here in the quarters. Well, I stayed out here in the quarters. At the Pigpen. I played at the Caliente Club. I played at the Catniff Fiddle. For Hip, it got the famous door.
Oh yeah, the famous door. Gendley.
And the, let's see, Gasper.
Oh yeah, I remember that.
And for Miss Valente at the Paddy. I played at the Palm Garden. I played for Mr. Dan at his club when he had his club right over there.
Tuluse.

Toulouse Street. The Gaslight, Tony Bessinas. The Dreamland for Sam, Sam and Selma. I played at the Village Bar. I played at the Spotlight. I played at the, I played with Fat Pichon a while at the Absinthe House. Oh, I played a lot of places. Oh, I think I would. Did you ever play any brass band work on the street much? One time. Really? I played a funeral over the river. And I. Whose band was it? That was, I think it was Howard.
Howard had the brass band. Oh, Kidd, I thought it might have been the old man Allen's band.
Well, I mean Allen played in the band, but he had got Howard to hire some of the musicians
from over here.

Yeah. That's right. Red Allen's there. I never got to see him, I'm sorry. We walked, I tell you, it looked like to me, it must have been around about ten miles there in the gravel. It was a cemetery up at McDonald's.
That's where we went to.
It was hot too.
It's a long ways, yeah. Boy.

Now, the next thing I played, the last carnival parade I played was with a minor, a minor's band. We played for the corner club. And that stopped me from playing parades. Right there, put it down. All day long. I got soaked wet in the rain three or four times that day.
Yeah, those carnival parades can go all day. It's a tough job.
I'll put it down.

I wonder, can you think of any other old-time drummers when you were a boy or younger on parades that you ever followed? Maybe you didn't even know their name, but can you think of any that you remember that you used to like and follow?
Well, I can't think too many of the fellas that was in those marching bands. Of course, I knew a lot of them,
but right offhand, right now,
or I think like or Chani and I remember when Dog Happy died. I mean, the one that died. I remember when he... Wait a minute.
Is he dead? The one they call Black Happy?
He used to study all the time. Goldston. Goldston, yeah.
After Goldston, he died. You remember Black Benny? Black Benny. He was based on one. I remember Black Benny.
I sure do.
I never got to see him. Louis Armstrong talks a lot about him.
Black Benny.
Another bass drummer, Trepanier. Did you ever see him?
I don't remember him. He might have been downtown more. Most likely I've seen him, but I mean, I don't remember.

No. And Cottrell, too. You know, Louis Cottrell's dad was a famous drummer. Probably worked most of the time downtown here. You might go ahead with your different shows now, because I know you played so many in some of the... Oh, yeah.
We had a gang of shows.
Can you remember? It doesn't have to be in any special order which one you went to next. I know you can't always remember that.
No.
Can you remember some of the names of the other shows or stars?
Well, yeah. J.C. Lincolent's Mighty Minstrel Show, Nailer's Mighty Minstrel.
These minstrel shows, were those mostly for colored or white audiences that you had then?
Well, they were colored and white.
Either one.
Colored and white audience.
Whenever you'd be on the road, you'd just...

That's right. Colored and white. You see, you'd play the main show, and then after the show there would be a concert for featuring a blues singer or something like that. You had to have a special act for the concert, you see?
Yeah.
Because they would always charge extra for the concert.
You see?
Well, now, the last show, the last minstrel show I was with was, I think that was in 1937. When I was with Brobby Rastus, that's the same show that Bessie Smith was on.
Yeah.
See? And we were together, I mean, when she...
Yeah, that's what I want to ask you in detail, if you don't mind telling that, because there'd been several rumors, you know, published. Well, some of the people...
It was 1937 that she was killed. 1937. Now, let's see, it was in 37. We were, we had about three more weeks off before we were going in.
If you don't mind, start at the beginning, when did you get into this show, and was she, was Bessie the star of it when you joined it, or how was it?
Well, Bessie met us on the, she came to the show, I was already on the show.
Yeah.
When she came to the show, she came to the show... It was called the Broadway... Broadway Rastus.
Broadway Rastus.
It was a show that belonged to Old Man Winstead, E.S. Winstead, out of Fayetteville, North Carolina.
Yeah.
So he had two shows on the road, see, and he had a guy managing this show that Bessie was on, see.
Yeah.

Bessie used to do concerts on the show, see. I and her husband were there together, you know. And we had about, oh, I imagine around about two more weeks out, I would say, before closing, see, because it was getting cold, you know, we were in there playing the Delta, the little towns in the Delta, Mississippi. And it was, you played in those smaller towns on a Saturday night because on a Saturday all the people mostly would come to town to get their groceries
and things, you know, a big crowd with wagons and horses and everybody wanted to see

the show that night. And this was in Darling, Mississippi that we played that night. And after the show it rained. So I used to drive the bus, you know, extra, with 35 people on the bus and the fellas, I mean, some of the fellas used to drive, like drive a truck or something, make extra money to keep them high and extra help, you see. And, well, Bessie and them used to leave ahead of us, you see.
They'd leave in the car. They'd leave in the car.
No, they had a nice, they had a packet.
Yeah, but I mean, it wasn't, they didn't drive on the bus, I mean, no, they rode in the car,

see. Her husband drove, I mean, she rode along with him, see. And they had a pink packet, nice little car. And they were about, I imagine, about an hour ahead of us, an hour, hour and a half ahead of us. When we were leaving there, we were going to, to Highlands, Highlandsdale, Mississippi, you see.
Yeah.
And we had showed this town, uh, uh, Clarksdale before, see, so we were supposed to pass through Clarksdale.
Yeah.
Well, this accident happened around about ten miles out of Clarksdale before you get to Clarksdale,
you see.

In between Memphis and Clarksdale where it happened. And, uh, riding, uh, in this car, well, when we got there, I mean, she was laying in the, you know, I mean, they had her laying out waiting for an ambulance to come pick up. I mean, I imagine she probably was dead then, you know, because she had bled so much.
She wasn't conscious at least. No, she wasn't conscious.
She didn't even know what was happening. It seemed though she had her arm out the window, you know, riding alone or home out the window.
I'd heard that too.
Sitting in there.
A lot of people do that.
And one of these seed trucks, you understand, was going the same way they were going.
Yeah, and passed.
That's right. And, uh, I think, uh, her husband tried to, to pull up, you know what I mean, to pull in front of the seed truck.
Yeah.
It was the way it seemed like it was, see. And her arm hit the seed truck and, I mean, it just, just pulled it off, just a little bit was,
barely hanging on.

Well, now, we tried to, I mean, they tried because we were behind them, you see, when this happened. We got there, well, see, they went over there to a farm, one of those farm houses to try to call an ambulance from Clarksdale to take her to the hospital. But they claimed they didn't have no ambulance there to take a colored person. They found out she was colored. They said they didn't have no ambulance to take her. I mean, they tried to put in a car or something. Well, they couldn't put in a car, you know, in the condition that she was in. You understand? So they had to call Hayes and Langston's undertaken up at, uh, Memphis. Memphis.
Which was around
about 90 and some miles.
Yeah.
Maybe a hundred miles.
Yeah, that's a long way.
So by the time Hayes and Langston's got there, well, I mean, she was dead.
Yeah. You see?
So all they could do then was just take the body.
Yeah.
Well, I read in magazines where it said they run into a tractor and a tractor run into, all that kind of humbug.
That wasn't it.
I happened to be there and I know.
Yeah. They just were passing a seed truck. Passing a seed truck.
You know, during the time that those people was harvesting their cotton, you know? Yeah. Cotton haulers up there and those trucks bringing those seeds to the mill.
Oh yeah. It's like one of those big, almost like a big trailer thing that looks so long. That's right.
One of those kind of things. Yeah, the eyes. They put a lot of seeds
in their truck. Yeah, I've seen those up in that part.
Well, that's the thing. That's what happened to her. And believe it or not, the last number she sang that night was, This is My Last Affair.
Yeah.
That's the last number she sang and she really sang it too.
Well, I heard her that same year, I guess, maybe in the spring of the year before she died, up at the Apollo. She'd be there a couple times a year and once at the Harlem Opera House.
That's right. That's a funny thing, Mr. Bill.
She could really sing.

That same morning when I was pulling out, there's a little grocery store that was next to the lot where we were parked. We had a bus where the couples stayed. There was, let's see, one, two, three, four, five, six, eight couples that stayed on this bus. They opened the bus up and made compartments for two couples around here and then two up here and so forth to keep from going around looking for rooms
and things, you see.
Well, this man next door at the grocery store, a white fellow next door, he told me that he kind of opened the store early that morning before we left so we could get cigarettes
and maybe we could get

I went up on the porch, you know, a little porch. The man had the light in the store and I wanted to knock on the door so he could open up, you see, let me in. So here come a fellow, a white fellow, you know, he come along there like he was drunk, you know, a man, he wobbling all around so he wanted to know what I was doing up there. So I told him I was waiting for the man to open the door for me to come in and get something to eat. He told me to get away from there. I said, well, I mean, I'm with the show. And he said, oh, you're with the show? I said, yeah. He said, you dance, huh? I said, no, I'm not a dancer. I said, I'm a musician, a drummer. He said, all you people can dance, all you kind of people can dance. I said, you're going to dance this morning.
Yeah, I've heard people like that.
So he pulled out
a pistol,
you know, and he shot down in the floor, you know. Man, you ought to see me dancing. I danced that morning.
Yeah, I see.

So he had a pipe, one of the four pints, he had drank some out of it, you know. Only then he told me to take a drink. Well, I mean, I take my drink and he drank behind me, you know what I mean? And he told me to go ahead and keep the rest of it and give me a dollar for dancing.
That's Mississippi for you. Well, now, he drank behind me. He wanted, you know, he was shooting me, but he still knows. He drank behind me. I don't know. You can't figure what people's on. I've done.
Yes, indeed.
Well, I think of it, who else was in the band in that show? Can you think of anybody else that, anybody else from New Orleans or anyone? Yeah. Well, no,
we had a couple of fellas from New Orleans that was on the show, but they had left us about a week before that. One was Joe Snayee. He's dead now. He was trumpet player.
He was in San Francisco, I guess. Yeah. Before he died.
No, he died here. Here. Well, then it was a father and a son both.
I never knew them.

Well, Joe Snayee, he died. Well, he was a trumpet player. Well, he left us about a week before that. And then the same Clement Turblin that plays trombone around at the paddock. Well, he was on the show, too. And he left. He and Joe left us together. They left in Memphis, you see, and came on home. You were heading south then? We were heading south. In other words, we was going to end up in Mississippi, and then we were going to leave from there and go back to North Carolina, going to Fayetteville for winter quarters, you see. That's right.
And you say, Bessie just sang in the concert then.
That's right. She sang.
And they had the whole band with her then?
Oh, yeah. The band had to play
the big show
and the concert, too. You see, the band had to play both.
How big a band was it? Can you remember
how many different instruments were? We had about 12 pieces. Oh, a big band like that? A big band. You had to put on
many parades or just play for the show?
Yeah, you had the parade. Yeah, a parade, too. See, every day you would have to make at least two or three circles, they called it, you see, let the people know the show was entirely.
Let's advertise the show.
You see, a lot of times, I mean, you just get in town, I mean, you just have to put on your uniform right quick and get out there.
The drummer start off, you know what I mean,
and you start walking and the comedians, you know, go along with the parade. Then at night, you had to make at least about two circles at night in town.
But they used a...
Bass drum too? Somebody else played bass drum?
Oh yeah, snare. I always played the snare and somebody else would play the bass.
About what instruments did they use then for the orchestra? Say accompanying Bessie for instance, about a couple of trumpets or how many?

We had three trumpets at one time. They had three saxophones and of course a couple of them double clarinet, the bass horn, two trombones. Then I played the traps, see, for sure I had to play the traps. The bass drummer mostly would be one of the comedians or something like that.
Somebody just doubled on the bass drum.
They doubled on the bass, you see. And they had a piano. They had a piano player.
Sometimes a piano player would play the bass drum, you see.
And then sometimes the piano player wouldn't be able to play the bass. Well they'd get one of the comedians or somebody like that.
Yeah. This wasn't a carnival show then that Bessie was with. It was just...

Oh, a minstrel show. See, it's different between... A minstrel. A minstrel, you could call it one-nighters. You see, a minstrel played one-nighters. On a carnival show you had a minstrel show too, but they used to call it a jig show.
Why they called it a jig show is on the kind of jigging they call it, and they used to call it a jig show, you see. Yeah.

And well, I mean they had different shows like the ten and one athletic show and so forth, and the Hawaiian show, and the jig show. Yeah. But now, on a minstrel show, most of the time they used a car, you see. You have a special railroad car, you see. And maybe two or three trucks that, you know, with this particular show...
Yeah, they'd carry a lot of things like rides and Ferris wheels and things like that, I guess. Well, that's on the carnival, you see.
Yeah, on the carnival. Well now, a minstrel show only carried a show, that's all. Just a big top.
Yeah. In a tent then.
In a tent.
You always have a tent with you then. That's right.

Now this old man, old man Palmer, it was his show, see. Well he had a car, and he sold a car, see. And he started using trucks. He figured, I mean, it'd be cheaper using trucks and bus to all the people, instead of using it, because railroad cars cost a lot of money. I mean, even to pull a car, man, out and transport from one track to another, and all that kind of stuff, I mean, it cost a lot of money. It's like circus. Yeah.

This reel is just about over. I was going to ask about the show again. In this show that Bessie Smith is with, everybody traveled in the bus then except Bessie, or were there some more cars too? Well, the stage manager, he had a car.
He and his wife. That's right. He had a car. And that was a tent show then, that first had the minstrel show, then after that would be the concert.

See, everybody would leave out. They'd have to leave the tent, then they'd pay to get back in again. They'd pay to come back in. Which used to be sometime 25 or made it 35 cents, according to what towns you were in, you know
the name, what you get. You remember any of the songs that Bessie sang in particular on that last trip? You mentioned the one song, the last one you sang.
Well, this was my last affair.
The last one. Were there any other blues or any particular songs?

Well, yeah, she sang a lot of blues, of course. She sang a lot of blues, but... She was just saying... She sang a lot of blues, of course, but... She was just saying... She sang the... TV blues. She sang the TV blues. She sang the TV blues.
She sang the TV blues. She sang the Deaf Letter Blues, Pink Slip Blues, One Hour Mama.
Oh yeah, I remember. That's one of the last things I heard her sing. One Hour Mama. One minute papa, I've got no use for you.
That's right. I remember that. Oh, it's another song by Something in the Park. Something in the Park. I forget what it was.
Of course, she made a lot of records of, I guess, a lot of the songs she made records of, she'd sing in her shows then too, people would want to hear.
One Sweet Letter from You.
I've never heard her sing that.
Different songs like that.

Some of the pop tunes too she'd sing then. When I'd hear at the Harlem Opera House or at the Apollo, she'd usually sing almost always just blues, is about all they wanted to hear. And I liked the blues too, I was happy to hear just blues. I'm going to ask any more about the show. What time did that happen? I mean about Bessie, you know. It was real late at night, you say, wasn't it? No, it was early in the morning.
Well, that's what I mean, yeah.
Early in the morning and four days during the dark.

Yeah, that's right. It was daylight. It should have been at least around about, must have been around about 4.30 or 5 o'clock. Yeah. It was around about that because, you know, how it is, I mean, in the time when it's, it seemed like the fall is coming, you know, how it looks that time of morning. It was just about maybe 4.30 or probably 5 o'clock in the morning.

Yeah. Anything else about that show that you can think of while we're on that, if you can think of anything else about the whole company, the other acts or anything in the minstrel show too? Now, Bessie was never in the minstrel part of it though. She didn't sing anything in that. No, see. No.
See, on the, in the concert, well, they had a couple of acts, you know, that they would do, you know, to make the concert a little longer, you know.
Sort of like in between, while she'd rest, they'd put on something else. That's right.
See, and they'd bring her on maybe before the last act, you see. And after she'd come on, then the last act, and that was it, you see.
Yeah.
Now, the other thing, I mean, she used to like to play tonk, you know. Yeah.
Yeah, she used to like her chords, you know, that's one thing.
Now, my former wife was on that show with me when she died. She lives back on St. Philip Street.
Now, she remembers too, but she's right there.
That's right. Aunt Bessie was pretty good friend, you know. Yeah. And she was a chorus girl.

Did Bessie seem in pretty good health? I never did know Bessie Smith except to see her on the stage. Oh, yeah, she was a good one. She seemed in still good health. She was. When I last saw her, she looked good, you know. She was always pretty heavy, but it seemed... She was in pretty good health. Good health and spirits as far as I could tell. That's right. She wasn't really so old either. No. I think, you know, maybe around 40 or something. That's right.
She used to like her little juice, of course. We used to always get our little bottles together.
A lot of people did, yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Oh, I was going to ask about Ida Cox. Did you ever tour with her?
Oh, yes, indeed. I was with Ida Cox in 1940.

That's what I'd heard, yeah. I wanted to hear you tell us about that. We still have time to talk a few minutes about her, if you don't mind. I was with Ida in the 40, and we left away from here. What show was that? Any particular name? Dogtown Scandals Review. Yeah. Where was they located, the winter quarters?
Well, Ida didn't have any special winter quarters then. You know, her home was in Knoxville, Tennessee. Ida Cox.
Yeah.
Well, she didn't have any special place of winter then, I mean because ...
I mean the show, though. Was she just with the show, or did she own the show? It was her show. What was her show?

She had Jack Skank was booking her. Jack Skank was out of New York. He was out of Brooklyn. He and his son was on the show, you know, managing the show. Jew. And I tell you, the show went along pretty good for a while, and we had our bad moments too. Nice, I mean ...

What years, can you figure out about what years? You were with Bessie, that would be in 1937, I guess, when she died. Were you with Ida then, you say, in 1940? 1940. 1940. Did you just start with her then?
Yeah, I started with Ida.

Because I was wondering, I first heard Ida Cox in St. Louis, a little theater up in the colored section, in 1938. I happened to be going through, I didn't know she was there. And one night I was walking up the street and saw ... Regal Theater. Yeah, I don't even remember the name, in St. Louis, out there. That's right. Some place I got on Del Mar, out in that section in there somewhere. I don't remember exactly. That's right.
We played the theater again, you see, we stayed there ...
Did you ever go to St. Louis with her? Yeah, we stayed in St. Louis about five months.
Oh really? That's right. In other words, you call me, we were stranded there.
You wouldn't have been there in 1938 then. No, this was in ... I didn't hear you then. That's right, this was in 1940.
Yeah. So we stayed at the Calumet Hotel, on Jefferson. We left St. Louis when we did leave there, we jumped from St. Louis to Kansas City.
Yeah.
Kansas City, Missouri. And we stayed around Kansas City about three weeks, playing in and out of Kansas City.
Did you ever know a drummer there who came from this part of the country, Baby Lovett? Well yeah. Used to play with Julia Lee, I guess you met him.
Well yeah, well I told him about the Lee, I played with Julia's brother. Julia played piano in the band when I was with her brother.
Oh really? Yeah, I know they had a band. Yeah. They made a record. That's right.
I even remember Count Beardsy before he had his big band. Count used to play in a little club that used to be called a Grotto Club.
Yeah, I've heard about those days in Kansas City. That's right.

Yeah, I played with George E. Lee as Julia's brother. Yeah. And Julia was playing piano in the band then because Jesse Stone had quit. That was his original piano player, Jesse Stone. Yeah, I was in the band for George E. Lee's band.
How long were you around that section?

Well, I stayed with, let's see, I was with George about, oh it must have been around about six or seven months. I stayed out at George's place. I used to live out on Forest, you know where Forest Street is. Yeah. I used to stay out on Forest and while I was with Ida, well we stayed around there around about, oh I guess about four, maybe five weeks, maybe more than that. We went out and come back, you know. Yeah. Go out and come back into Kansas City.
And you stayed in St. Louis a long time. Well, about five months in St. Louis.
Yeah.
How long were you with Ida Cox?

Well, I stayed with Ida almost a year. I left Ida and Charleston, West Virginia. I mean not in Charleston, but in Huntington. We played Charleston and I left from Charleston, we went to Huntington. Yeah. And we played Huntington and I left Ida and Huntington, West Virginia. And I stayed around Huntington, I guess around about a month. Then I went back to Charleston and I started playing with a band in Charleston. Well, I stayed there on about six weeks. And I left from then and came on to Charlotte, North Carolina.

I was going to ask what kind of a, what else was on this show. It's funny, I can't even remember. I don't know how you can remember all that. I can't even remember to 38. All I can remember is Ida Cox singing several songs and she was the main attraction in the whole bill. That's right. But I don't know if there was many other acts or a movie. I don't even remember if it was a movie or what it was there.
Yeah, I mean she had a nice show.
A really nice show. It wasn't entirely her show as far as I remember that she was just like a special act brought into the theater. I thought maybe it was all her show.
Well this show was her. Ida Cox's Dogtown Scandals Review.
And it took the whole evening, the whole...
We had a bus and everything. The whole performance.

I mean it wasn't just a part of the show, it was the whole thing. The whole thing, that's right. And you all traveled by bus. By bus, we had a bus. They have other acts and dancers and other singers I guess. That's right.
I think one time we had this boy play, Lonnie Johnson was on the show.
Oh, he was. I knew him in Chicago, out west.

He left us in Pickway, Ohio. He was on the show. And we had another guy with a bicycle act. He used to take the bicycle, just ride one wheel and all that kind of stuff. He was called Chief Somebody. I forget his name. He was on the show. Yeah, chorus girls we had with my wife in... Oh, one, two, three, four. We had about four or five girls from here in the Walnut. On the show.

Well, I think I would keep changing the subject maybe, but since you, I know, sing so well and do a lot of singing with George Lewis' band, did you ever sing in any of those shows? Oh yeah, I used to sing. You would sing too?
I used to have my specialties, you know, like the band played the overture, you know, play overture. I used to sing maybe two or three numbers.
Would you still play your drums or get out in front and sing? I'd still play my drums.
Still play your drums. And sing. Put the mic by me, you know, me and I'd sing the same way.

Well, let's see if there's anything else about Ida Cox that I can ask you, or that you can remember, about her, what song she featured. I know she made quite a few old Paramount records and then, in the, about 1940 or so, along that time, she made a couple more in New York. That's right. She went there and sang once at a concert in New York. That's right. But do you remember what song she featured on the show or anything?

Well, I tell you now, she made a, she sang a lot of the same songs like Bessie sang. Yeah. You know, like I said Death Letter Blues, Pink Slip Blues, One Hour Mama and all those kind of numbers. She sang the same thing.
And you know, some pop songs, I mean, she sang.

Because, you see, we had another girl, I used to sing most of the pop tunes, they called Annette Bailey, a girl from Birmingham, Alabama. She was a nice singer too. I haven't, I don't know what happened to her, Annette, but she was a nice singer too.
Yeah.
And, well, Ida used to feature her too, you know.
You think Ida was older than Bessie or younger? Could you tell? I mean, I never can judge people's age.
I think Ida was a little older than Bessie.

I thought maybe she might be too. Yeah. She was a little older than Bessie. I didn't know. Did Ida ever use a microphone? I know Bessie ordinarily didn't bother with the microphone, had such a big voice. I never heard Ida Cox, but about, oh I did hear in New York at a club too, Cafe Society, with Edmund Hall's band. Yeah. She was there one winter, just part of the winter, maybe a month or so. She된 stuff
I didn't remember. I got caught out tonight.

Yeah, I guess we better be finishing up. If there's anything you can think of and real important about your life, I guess you've covered most of it as far as your show work and your early days. That's the main thing we were wondering about because we're trying to study that old history and you might say preserve it so it won't be forgotten. Anything else that you can think of real quickly that you might have left out that you'd want to put on here?

Well, I'll tell you, I would have to think. There's a lot of things, I mean, like different circuses and so forth like that. I mean, like different things I could talk about. I'll tell you what I said, but it takes you time to think. Yeah, I know, that's right. You were with circuses then too.
I was with everything that you could mention.
I had a little music. That's right. I even had ten pieces in the service when I was in there.
Oh, really? In an army. Where was that? Over in France.
Over in France. I was in both theaters. Over in France, Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, and down in the Pacific, Okinawa, Korea, Japan, Panama.

We were traveling all over again. That's right. Well, I think we better, it won't be late setting up your drums. I'll turn it off. Yeah. This interview ended after about one and a half reels since Dave Oxley had to play next door at Preservation Hall the night of January the 6th. So the balance of this reel will conclude the interview of James Sing Miller, his interview of December 11th, 1964.

segments.title: Opening and birth in Carrollton
segments.summary: Bill Russell identifies the interview (Jan 6, 1965) and Oxley gives his name and birth in Carrollton, 1910.

segments.title: Family, early music and Carrollton
segments.summary: No musicians in his family, though they were singers; he followed parades and second lines as a boy and lived around Carrollton.

segments.title: Drumming on the steps and first drum set
segments.summary: He began beating on box steps with chair rounds at six or seven and bought his first drum set at about fourteen.

segments.title: Playing along with records at family fish fries
segments.summary: He learned by playing along with Celestin and Oliver records, and played at his mother's Saturday fish fries.

segments.title: Schooling at McDonogh 24
segments.summary: No school music; he attended McDonogh No. 24 in Carrollton, possibly Mahalia Jackson's school.

segments.chapter: Early jobs and Johnny Lee Long show
segments.title: First job at Milneburg with Chris Kelly
segments.summary: At almost fifteen he worked at a dry dock, then played Milneburg on Sundays with Prince Miller, Bubba Green and Chris Kelly's band.

segments.chapter: Early jobs and Johnny Lee Long show
segments.title: Favorite drummer Red Happy and early bands
segments.summary: His favorite drummer was Red Happy of the Lyric Theater; he played with Kid Howard before going on the road.

segments.chapter: Early jobs and Johnny Lee Long show
segments.title: Touring with Johnny Lee Long on TOBA
segments.summary: He left in 1926, at nearly sixteen, with Johnny Lee Long's show on the TOBA circuit through southern cities, Chicago and Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Early jobs and Johnny Lee Long show
segments.title: Pay and drum stunts on the show
segments.summary: He was the only New Orleanian, started at $18 a week, and got a raise to $25 for his drum act copying Happy's tricks.

segments.title: Miller's Midway carnival show and Willie Humphrey Sr.
segments.summary: He spent about two years with Miller's carnival, with Calvin Distance, Jazz Baby and bandleader Willie Humphrey Sr. on clarinet.

segments.title: Seven years away and return to New Orleans bands
segments.summary: After seven years east on the road, he came home and played with Kid Howard, Henry Russ, Henry Horton and Jimmy Davis.

segments.title: Clubs played in New Orleans
segments.summary: He lists clubs he played, including the Robin Hood, Rhythm Club with Joe Robichaux, the Famous Door, Dreamland and Absinthe House.

segments.title: A brass band funeral and last carnival parade
segments.summary: He once played a funeral over the river with Howard's brass band, and a long Mardi Gras parade ended his parade playing.

segments.title: Old parade drummers
segments.summary: Russell asks about early parade drummers; Oxley recalls Happy, Black Benny and others vaguely, not Trepagnier.

segments.title: Minstrel shows and concerts
segments.summary: He names minstrel shows he toured with, their mixed audiences, and the extra-charge concert after the main show.

segments.title: Bessie Smith's show and the night before her death
segments.summary: He joined Broadway Rastus, Winstead's show, with Bessie Smith; they played Darling, Mississippi, and she and her husband left ahead in a car.

segments.title: Bessie Smith's fatal accident
segments.summary: He describes the crash near Clarksdale, the delay in getting an ambulance, her death, and corrects magazine versions.

segments.title: Mississippi grocery store encounter
segments.summary: On the morning before the accident, a drunk white man with a pistol made him dance, then gave him a drink and a dollar.

segments.title: Band size and parades on the Bessie Smith show
segments.summary: Two New Orleans players had left; the band backed Bessie, played the show and concert, and paraded daily.

segments.chapter: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
segments.title: Instrumentation of the show band
segments.summary: The twelve-piece band had three trumpets, three saxes, two trombones, bass horn and piano; comedians doubled on bass drum.

segments.chapter: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
segments.title: Minstrel versus carnival shows
segments.summary: He explains minstrel one-nighters versus carnival jig shows, tents, trucks and railroad cars, and the concert admission.

segments.title: Bessie Smith's songs and time of the accident
segments.summary: He recalls her last song and repertoire, and that the accident was around 4:30 or 5 a.m.

segments.title: Concert structure and Bessie Smith as a person
segments.summary: Bessie was only in the concert, liked to play tonk and drink, and Oxley's then-wife was a chorus girl on the show.

segments.chapter: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
segments.title: Joining Ida Cox in 1940: St. Louis and Kansas City
segments.summary: With Ida Cox's Dogtown Scandals Review in 1940 he was stranded five months in St. Louis, then worked around Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
segments.title: Playing with George E. Lee in Kansas City
segments.summary: He played six or seven months with George E. Lee's band, with Julia Lee on piano, and remembers Basie at the Grotto Club.

segments.chapter: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
segments.title: Leaving Ida Cox and the Dogtown Scandals show
segments.summary: He stayed almost a year, left in Huntington, West Virginia; the show had Lonnie Johnson, a bicycle act and chorus girls.

segments.chapter: Minstrel show life and Ida Cox
segments.title: Oxley's singing and Ida Cox's repertoire
segments.summary: He sang specialties on the show; Ida Cox sang the same blues as Bessie and featured singer Annette Bailey.

segments.title: Closing remarks and military service
segments.summary: Russell wraps up; Oxley mentions circuses and army service in Europe and the Pacific; the tape note says he had to play Preservation Hall.
